children.text:
It makes me curious whether vendoring/reimplementing dependencies is actually, in an odd way, optimal for these frontier proofs.

I've certainly seen that when doing normal coding, LLMs will often take documentation of used libraries at face value, and try to save context by not reading the underlying implementations into context. This is genuinely useful!

But for math, is there a use to a set of agents being forced to reimplement the entire stack of formalized dependencies? Each sub-effort would leave artifacts, and send messages to other sessions, on ways in which the underlying mechanics or subtleties might prove helpful to the broader effort. No need to fight terseness with system prompts, when a full survey of the broader field is impossible to avoid.

They've been working on it, but there are centuries of maths to formalise and it's not trivial. Maths papers are kind of... hand-wavy, in a way. Getting a piece of machinery into Lean requires making everything absolutely concrete, down to the lowest level of detail, and some of the objects involved are very complex, built upon layers and layers of abstraction.

Kevin Buzzard is a prominent mathematician who's been working on formalising FLT in Lean (https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT/blob/main/GENER...). He was one of the first mathematicians I encountered leading the charge on this, many many years before LLMs.

There's a _lot_ of groundwork to build. But it's getting easier now of course.

children.author: BLanen
children.text:
In my opinion, it does, but it needs more than that. But it already has a package manager(lake) and the main package all these mathematical proofs and definitions and such are contributed to is mathlib.

I would argue it needs something like content-addressed code/"packages" like the newish programming language unison. But it also needs more than that even. I would argue that a (cubical)-HoTT language/environment/proof-assistant is probably better for the future of mathematical research because it does not have "proof irrelevance" and does not treat different proofs as equals because they often take different "paths" and those paths are often interesting and analysable in themselves. I also would argue that it needs to have a sort of decentralised way of certifying computations of proofs that goes beyond the ad-hoc way they are currently done in lean/mathlib.

These are all not original points by me but have often been stated as a sort of criticism of lean/math-lib(although I acknowledge them as a massively successful and admirable engineering feats) by other people way more knowledgable than me.

Does that mean lean community needs a package manager of sorts? So that it can import all these as pre-proven packages that they collectively build on. I can't imagine this to be something that they already haven't thought of or done in some form.

Ideally they sholuld be able to just do a `import riemann_hypothesis;` from a verified registry and then build on that.

children.author: Zambyte
children.text:
Code golfing often measures by character count or things like that, which leads to hard to understand results due to short symbol naming. This seems avoidable by measuring by something other than character count.

It also leads to hacks taking advantage of underlying hardware or runtime quirks, which are anything but easy to follow. I don't know Lean, but it seems like it wouldn't expose abstractions that would allow for these kinds of hacks either.

If there was a challenge that was something like "provide GRH in the fewest Lean symbols", that seems like it could produce comprehensible results.
I agree with the sentiment, but there are competitions to do things with the shortest amount of code in other programming languages, and it does not lead to anything simple or understandable.
